tldr:
The **Message Batches API** costs **50% less**, but runs asynchronously: up to **24 hours**, **no latency guarantee**.

- **Batch it:** latency-tolerant, non-blocking work (overnight reports, weekly audits, nightly test generation).
- **Keep synchronous:** **blocking** checks (pre-merge), and workflows that need **tool results mid-request**.

**Running a batch well:**

- Give every request a unique **`custom_id`** and match results by it, because order isn't guaranteed.
- **Resubmit only failures**, fixing the cause (e.g. chunk over-long documents).
- Pick a submission window so **window + 24 h ≤ SLA** (4 h for a 30 h SLA).
- **Refine the prompt on a sample** before sending thousands.
mentalModel: The batch API is the overnight post: half the price, delivered sometime within a day, in no particular order. Put a label (custom_id) on every envelope so you know which reply belongs to which letter. Don't post anything someone is standing at the counter waiting for — or any letter that needs a reply before it can be finished.
whatItIs:
The exam guide covers designing efficient batch processing (Guide §6 · TS 4.5, pp.18–19). The batch-processing docs give the
exact limits and result types.

**Sub-concepts — each with its picture to remember**

| # | Sub-concept | 🧭 Mental model | ⭐ Exam reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 50% cheaper, up to 24 h, no SLA | Overnight post: cheap, arrives within a day. | ⭐ TS 4.5 · Knowledge 1 |
| 2 | Blocking vs latency-tolerant | Nobody waits at the counter for overnight post. | ⭐ TS 4.5 · Knowledge 2, Skill 1 |
| 3 | No mid-request tool loop | A letter that needs a reply before it's finished can't go by post. | ⭐ TS 4.5 · Knowledge 3 |
| 4 | `custom_id` | A label on every envelope — replies arrive in any order. | ⭐ TS 4.5 · Knowledge 4 |
| 5 | Resubmit only failures (fixed) | Re-post only the letters that came back — trimmed if they were too heavy. | ⭐ TS 4.5 · Skill 3 |
| 6 | Cadence from the SLA | Post often enough that waiting plus delivery fits the promise. | ⭐ TS 4.5 · Skill 2 |
| 7 | Sample first | Proof-read one letter before printing ten thousand. | ⭐ TS 4.5 · Skill 4 |
| 8 | Result types | Delivered · returned (errored) · cancelled · expired — only delivered ones are billed. | 📘 docs |

**Message Batches API vs synchronous Messages API** (the comparison CLAUDE.md requires)

| # | Aspect | Message Batches API | Synchronous Messages API |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Cost | ⭐ 50% of standard | Standard |
| 2 | Latency | ⭐ Most within 1 h, up to 24 h; no guarantee; expires after 24 h | Seconds |
| 3 | Use for | ⭐ Overnight reports, weekly audits, nightly test generation | ⭐ Blocking pre-merge checks, interactive work |
| 4 | Tool loop mid-request | ⭐ No — nothing returns tool results inside the request | Yes — the agentic loop |
| 5 | Correlation | ⭐ `custom_id`; results in any order | The response to your call |
| 6 | Failures | Per request: errored / expired (not billed); resubmit those | Per call: retry the call |
| 7 | Size limits | 100,000 requests or 256 MB per batch | One request |
| 8 | Results kept | 29 days | — |

**Submission cadence for an SLA** (batch processing up to 24 h)

| # | SLA | Largest window (SLA − 24 h) | Guide example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 30 h | 6 h | ⭐ 4 h windows (leaves margin) |
| 2 | 36 h | 12 h | — |
| 3 | 48 h | 24 h (once a day) | — |
howItWorks:
1. **Is someone waiting, or does the task need tool results mid-request?** Use the synchronous API. Otherwise, batch.
2. **Refine the prompt on a small sample** with the synchronous API; the docs also advise dry-running one request shape.
3. **Build requests** with a unique, meaningful `custom_id` (1–64 chars: letters, digits, `-`, `_`).
4. **Submit on a cadence** where window + 24 h fits the SLA.
5. **Read results by `custom_id`.** Resubmit only errored or expired ones, fixing the cause first (e.g. chunk over-long
   documents).

grounding.text: The Message Batches API processes requests asynchronously at 50% of the standard cost; most batches finish within an hour; results are available when all requests finish or after 24 hours; requests not processed within 24 hours expire.
grounding.ref: batch-processing § How it works; Batch limitations; Pricing

grounding.text: A batch holds up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB; results are available for 29 days.
Each request needs a unique custom_id (1–64 characters: letters, digits, - and _); results can be returned in any order — always match them with custom_id.
grounding.ref: batch-processing § Prepare and create; Retrieving results (note)

grounding.text: Result types: succeeded, errored (invalid request or server error — not billed), canceled, expired (not billed); one request's failure doesn't affect the others; implement retry logic for failed requests.
grounding.ref: batch-processing § Retrieving batch results; Best practices; Troubleshooting

grounding.text: Batches accept tool use, system messages and multi-turn conversation history, but each request is processed independently — there's no round trip for your code to run a tool and return its result within the request.
Best practices: meaningful custom_id values; break very large datasets into multiple batches; dry-run a single request shape with the Messages API to avoid validation errors.

Batch API: 50% cost savings, up to 24-hour processing, no latency SLA; suited to non-blocking, latency-tolerant work (overnight reports, weekly audits, nightly test generation), not blocking workflows (pre-merge checks); no multi-turn tool calling within a single request; custom_id correlates requests and responses.

Skills: sync API for blocking pre-merge checks, batch for overnight/weekly; compute submission frequency from the SLA (4-hour windows keep a 30-hour SLA with 24-hour processing); resubmit only failed documents by custom_id, e.g. chunking ones that exceeded context limits; refine the prompt on a sample before large batches.
The jobs, documents, failures, cost units and the effect of sample refinement are invented.

examPoints.text: Message Batches API: 50% cost savings, up to 24-hour processing, no guaranteed latency.
Batch suits non-blocking, latency-tolerant work (overnight reports, weekly audits, nightly tests), not blocking workflows (pre-merge checks).
No multi-turn tool calling within one batch request — tools can't run mid-request with results returned.
custom_id correlates each request with its response.
Match the API to latency needs: synchronous for blocking pre-merge checks, batch for overnight/weekly analysis.
Compute submission frequency from the SLA (4-hour windows keep a 30-hour SLA with 24-hour processing).
On failures, resubmit only the failed documents (by custom_id), with fixes such as chunking over-long documents.
Refine the prompt on a sample before batch-processing large volumes, to raise first-pass success.

variants.label: ✅ ⭐ sync for blocking & tool loops · batch for the rest · custom_id · resubmit failures · 4 h windows · sample first
variants.observe: premerge → sync. nightly → batch, 200 units instead of 400. results_order: results arrive shuffled; every summary is matched by custom_id. partial_failure: 5 resubmitted, DOC-00007 and DOC-00042 in chunks. sla_cadence: 4 + 24 = 28 h ≤ 30 h. tool_loop → sync, the agentic loop runs. sample_first: 97% first-pass, 300 re-dos.
variants.why: Each job goes where its latency and its need for tool results allow, and the batch is run with the docs' own practices.

variants.label: ⭐❌ A — a blocking pre-merge check in a batch
variants.observe: The PR check waits up to 24 h with no latency guarantee — merges are blocked.
variants.why: Batches are for non-blocking, latency-tolerant work; a blocking check needs the synchronous API.

variants.label: ⭐❌ B — matching results by position
variants.observe: Results arrive as DOC-00004, 00000, 00005 … — 5 of 6 documents get another document's summary.
variants.why: Batch results can come back in any order; custom_id is how requests and responses are correlated.

variants.label: ⭐❌ C — resubmitting the whole batch
variants.observe: 100 requests resubmitted to recover 5 — paying again for 95 that already succeeded.
variants.why: Only the failed documents, identified by custom_id, need resubmitting.

variants.label: ⭐❌ D — resubmitting too-long documents unchanged
variants.observe: DOC-00007 and DOC-00042 go back as they were — “prompt is too long” again.
variants.why: A failure caused by the document itself needs a change (the guide's example: chunking) before resubmitting.

variants.label: ⭐❌ E — submitting once a day for a 30 h SLA
variants.observe: A document arriving just after submission waits 24 h, then up to 24 h in the batch → 48 h > 30 h.
variants.why: Worst case = submission window + 24 h processing; the window must fit inside the SLA (the guide uses 4 h).

variants.label: ⭐❌ F — a tool-calling workflow in a batch
variants.observe: Each request ends at stop_reason tool_use — nothing runs the tool and sends the result back; 20 investigations stop half-way.
variants.why: A batch request can't have your code execute a tool mid-request and return the result.
variants.fix: Run tool loops on the synchronous API.

variants.label: ⭐❌ G — no sample refinement
variants.observe: The untested prompt goes to 10,000 tickets: 70% first-pass success, 3,000 need a second batch.
variants.why: Refining the prompt on a sample first raises first-pass success and cuts resubmission cost.
variants.fix: Iterate on a small sample (sync), then batch.

questions.q: A support team runs two Claude workloads: a live refund-eligibility check that the agent calls while the customer waits in chat, and a weekly quality report scoring the week's 8,000 transcripts. Finance asks to move both to the Message Batches API for the 50% saving. What is the right call?
opts: Move both, and tell chat customers that the answer will arrive by email within a day.
Move only the weekly quality report to batches; keep the live eligibility check synchronous.
Move only the live eligibility check, since it has the most requests and so saves the most money.
Keep both synchronous, and cut costs instead by moving both workloads to a smaller model.
questions.explain: Batches suit latency-tolerant work: they are 50% cheaper but can take up to 24 hours, with no latency guarantee. A customer waiting in chat can't wait that long, and a weekly report can. A breaks the live experience. C picks exactly the wrong workload. D ignores an easy saving on the weekly report.

questions.q: A batch of 500 document extractions comes back, and the team pairs each result with its input by its position in the results list. An audit finds 23 records holding another document's data, all from batches that included failed requests. What is the fix?
opts: Sort the results by completion time before pairing, so their order matches the submission order.
Submit batches of one request each, so there is only ever one result to pair with its input.
Give every request a custom_id, and match each result to its input by that custom_id.
Ask the model to repeat the document's filename in its output, and pair results by that text.
questions.explain: custom_id is the documented way to correlate batch requests with their results. Position isn't a reliable key. A still depends on order. B throws away the point of batching. D trusts generated text as an ID.

questions.q: In a nightly batch of 2,000 extractions, 40 requests failed, 12 of them because their documents exceeded the context limit. The current recovery script resubmits the entire batch of 2,000, which doubles the night's cost. What is the most efficient recovery?
opts: Resubmit only the 40 failures by custom_id, splitting the 12 over-long documents into chunks first.
Resubmit only the 40 failures by custom_id, unchanged, and repeat until every one of them succeeds.
Resubmit the entire batch as now, but with a larger max_tokens so the over-long documents will fit.
Process the 40 failures synchronously in a loop, retrying each one up to five times until it succeeds.
questions.explain: Resubmit only the failed requests, identified by custom_id, and fix what made them fail: the over-long documents need chunking. B resubmits 12 requests that will fail again. C re-runs 1,960 successful requests, and max_tokens limits output, not input. D retries the over-long documents unchanged.

questions.q: Documents arrive throughout the day, and each must be extracted within 30 hours of arriving. Batches can take up to 24 hours to process. The team submits one batch a day at midnight, and last month 9% of documents missed the deadline. How often should the team submit batches?
opts: Every 12 hours, since that halves the wait compared with the current daily schedule.
Once a day as now, but with an urgent flag on documents that arrived early in the day.
Every 24 hours, but moved to noon, when most of each day's documents have usually already arrived.
Every 4 hours, so the longest wait before submission plus processing stays within 30 hours.
questions.explain: Worst case = time waiting for the next submission + up to 24 hours of processing. Every 4 hours gives 4 + 24 = 28 hours, inside 30. A gives 12 + 24 = 36 hours. B invents a priority flag. C still leaves a wait of up to 24 hours.

questions.q: A nightly refund-review job needs the model to call lookup_order, see the result, then decide on each of 3,000 refunds. An engineer proposes running these as a Message Batch, one request per refund, to halve the cost. What is the problem?
opts: Batch requests can't include any tool definitions, so the model couldn't even ask for lookup_order.
3,000 requests is too many for one batch, so the job would need splitting into several batches.
There's no mid-request round trip, so the tool result can't come back for the model to continue.
Batch results arrive in random order, so refund decisions couldn't be matched to their orders.
questions.explain: A batch request is a single request with no chance to run a tool and return its result mid-request. A multi-turn tool loop doesn't fit inside one. A is not the point the guide makes: what's missing is the round trip. B isn't the issue here. D is solved by custom_id.

questions.q: A team is about to batch-process 100,000 archived contracts with a brand-new extraction prompt. Last year a similar run had to be redone entirely after the team found a date-format error on day two. What should they do first?
opts: Submit the full batch now, since the 50% saving makes a full rerun affordable if one turns out to be needed.
Refine the prompt on a representative sample until first-pass results are good, then submit the full batch.
Submit the full batch with a validation step, and resubmit only the contracts that fail that validation.
Split the 100,000 contracts into 100 batches and submit them all at once, so that each error affects less.
questions.explain: Refine the prompt on a sample before batch-processing a large volume, so problems are found cheaply. A bets on a costly rerun. C catches only errors that validation can see, such as a missing field, and misses semantic ones like a misread date format. D submits the same flawed prompt 100 times.

questions.q: Finance asks to move a weekly compliance audit of about 20,000 support transcripts to the Message Batches API. An engineer objects that results might arrive many hours later and that there is no latency guarantee. The audit report is due every Monday. What is the right assessment?
opts: Reject it, because a job with no latency guarantee should never be used for compliance reporting.
Accept it only if each request is resubmitted synchronously whenever it takes longer than an hour.
Reject it, because batch processing is designed for code tasks, not for reading support transcripts.
Accept it: 50% cheaper and up to 24 hours to process, with no guarantee, which suits a weekly audit.
questions.explain: The facts are a 50% saving, processing that can take up to 24 hours, and no latency SLA. A weekly deadline absorbs that easily. A rules batching out on a principle the facts don't support. B adds complexity for no need. C invents a restriction.

faq.q: The docs say batches support tool use and multi-turn conversations — doesn't that contradict the guide?
faq.a: No. A batched request can include tool definitions and earlier turns. What can't happen is the round trip: Claude asks for a tool, your code runs it, and the result goes back within the same request. Each request is processed on its own, so tool loops belong on the synchronous API.
The docs say errored, canceled and expired requests are not billed. Resubmitting only those keeps the cost at what you actually needed.

faq.q: Why 4-hour windows if the arithmetic allows 6?
faq.a: 30 − 24 = 6 is the limit with no slack. The guide's example uses 4 hours, leaving margin for queueing and resubmissions.

faq.q: How big can a batch be?
faq.a: Up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB, whichever comes first. The docs suggest splitting very large datasets into several batches.
